<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash narrowed properly, but A converted its two burdens into sharper, better-answered pressure. A's "name the judge" demand forced B to specify a verdict-maker; B's answer (regulators/audits using ghosting rates, time-to-match, complaint volume, analogized to predatory lending/gambling design) was reasonable, but A turned it cleanly — those proxies are engagement metrics in disguise, fast time-to-match is exactly what infinite decks produce, and low ghosting is what a small paywalled pool produces — plus the weighing that a regulator would end up mandating one romantic ideal over heterogeneous user goals. A also landed an unanswered internal contradiction: B's revenue substitute (extra likes, filters, read receipts) is itself paid visibility and preferential access, so B "renamed the toll booth" and left the underserved user with filters rather than a way to be seen. B's strongest move — the manipulation-blindness reframe ("you cannot vote with your feet against a manipulation you've been engineered not to notice") — genuinely undercut A's market-discipline story, and B's concession-mining on "the queue is ordered by prior engagement" was well-executed. But A defused both: engagement ranking as an imperfect proxy rather than a corrupted signal (mechanism description ≠ outcome verdict), and users demonstrably do perceive the problem ("swipe fatigue" as folk vocabulary, paid-user decline). B's closing, while rhetorically strong, recapped the perception argument without touching A's toll-booth turn or the regulator-metrics turn. A adapted more and left fewer live hits standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's second rebuttal turning B's proposed judge and revenue fix against it: B's audit proxies (time-to-match, ghosting) are themselves engagement metrics, while B's replacement revenue (extra likes, filters) is paid visibility under another name — leaving the underserved 45-year-old worse off. B's closing never answered either point.</best_rebuttal>
